newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hongkong Electric long-term future seen bright.
newsitem.headline: Hongkong Electric long-term future seen bright.

text.p: Hongkong Electric Holdings Ltd may achieve faster earnings growth after it comes under the wing of Cheung Kong Holdings Ltd group's infrastructure unit, although analysts see little improvement in the near term.
"The chief beneficiary of the restructuring will be Hongkong Electric and its shareholders," a local analyst said on Tuesday.

As part of the Cheung Kong group's restructuring announced on Monday, Hutchison Whampoa Ltd said it had acquired 7.75 million shares in the utility at HK$26.50 each, pushing its holding above 35.01 percent and triggering a general offer.

Under the proposed reorganisation, Hutchison is to transfer its 35.01 percent, and any other shares it receives in the general offer up to a 50.01 percent stake, to Cheung Kong Infrastructure Holding Ltd (CKI).
The shift in Hongkong Electric's ownership from diversified conglomerate Hutchison to infrastructure specialist CKI will help the utility in the long term, analysts said.

"Longer term, if they are successful in teaming up with CKI, this will solve the problem of low earnings growth," said Eric Savage, analyst at Salomon Brothers. But he said it would take time for the utility to see actual contributions to earnings.
Savage cited the long investment process of overseas power plant projects undertaken by independent power producers such as China Light & Power Ltd and Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd.

CKI is active in China toll bridge, toll road and power projects, and analysts said they expected to see Hongkong Electric play a greater role in Cheung Kong group's China and other overseas infrastructure development projects.
Near term, however, the change in controlling shareholder will not have any impact on the Hongkong Electric's earnings, said Anne Kao, research analyst at CS First Boston.
"We can't quantify the impact of the deal on Hongkong Electric," said Kao. "We can only say that the restructuring will have a conceptual benefit."
"The short-term impact on Hongkong Electric is rather neutral," said Salomon's Savage. "But the company should continue to operate under the scheme of control."
The utility company operates under a government-approved scheme of control, which regulates the profits and tariffs in respect of the generation and sale of electricity only.
The consensus forecast for Hongkong Electric is for zero earnings per share growth in 1996 and 10 percent in 1997, according to the Estimate Directory.
Kao is forecasting 10.0 percent earnings per share growth for Electric in 1997 and 7.0 percent in 1998.

In its mid-year interim earnings report, which showed a 14.3 percent decline in net profits on the year, the company said it expects a huge increase in demand for power, but not until 2003 when large infrastructure projects in Hong Kong come on line.
But some analysts doubt the utility will get a slice of lucrative CKI projects.
"I don't see why that should be the case. Hongkong Electric has always been part of the stable and it never got any projects before," said an analyst with a large overseas-based house.
"Even if CKI gets 50.01 percent, the lion's share of the profit is likely to be funnelled through 86-percent-held CKI to Hutchison."
Conditions of the deal, including shareholder and exchange approval, are expected to be fulfilled by May 31.
Following a one-day trading suspension, Hongkong Electric shares ended Tuesday up HK$2.40 at HK$27.65, well above Hutchison's general offer price of HK$26.50.
